### [Pour Decisions: Alcohol Privatization and Birth Outcomes](papers/Hall_JMP_v1.pdf){target="_blank"}

**Job Market Paper** · [PDF](papers/Hall_JMP_v1.pdf){target="_blank"}

<p class="paper-abstract">Alcohol-market liberalization can generate a large aggregate demand response without producing an equally large change in a particular externality if the behavioral response occurs outside the population relevant to that harm. I study Washington's Initiative 1183, which privatized spirits retailing in June 2012 and expanded entry by grocery and big-box stores. NielsenIQ Homescan data indicate that recorded conventional-spirits beverage volume increased by 71.4% following privatization. Complete ethanol quantities are not validated because product-level alcohol-content coverage is insufficient. These data do not identify consumers or prenatal alcohol exposure. Using restricted-use vital statistics and repeated-cross-section synthetic difference-in-differences, I estimate declines of 10.28 grams in average birth weight and increases of 0.274 and 0.357 percentage points in low birth weight and small-for-gestational-age births. These estimates are not unusually large relative to complete placebo-state refits, and the broader fetal-growth outcome family is not jointly unusual. Pregnancy accounting and maternal composition reveal no large, coherent shift in the observed birth pool. Within Washington, predetermined grocery infrastructure strongly predicts expansions in one-mile spirits access, but the associated birth-health estimates are mixed and sensitive to identification diagnostics. The results show that aggregate alcohol-demand responses alone are insufficient to predict a specific downstream harm: product substitution and the incidence of the behavioral response determine whether market liberalization reaches the relevant population.</p>

:::

<h3>Did Decriminalization Increase Overdoses?</h3>
<p class="paper-byline">David Hall, with Ben Hansen and Kyutaro Matsuzawa</p>
<p class="paper-links"><a href="https://www.nber.org/papers/w35427">NBER Working Paper No. 35427</a> · <a href="https://doi.org/10.3386/w35427">DOI</a> · <a href="https://ssrn.com/abstract=7063369">SSRN</a></p>
<p class="paper-abstract">We study drug decriminalization using Oregon's Measure 110 and Washington's <em>Blake</em> decision. Synthetic-control estimates show that both policies sharply reduced drug arrests and were followed by sustained increases in overdose mortality relative to matched counterfactuals. The estimates imply approximately 1,186 excess deaths in Oregon and 1,895 in Washington from 2021 through 2023. Alternative measures of fentanyl supply continue to yield positive overdose effects.</p>
</div>

### [Does Substance Use Treatment Still Reduce Mortality?](papers/Hall_Treatment_Mortality.pdf){target="_blank"}

**Under review at the Journal of Health Economics** · [PDF](papers/Hall_Treatment_Mortality.pdf){target="_blank"}

<p class="paper-abstract">This paper asks whether expanded substance use disorder treatment access continued to reduce overdose mortality as the opioid epidemic shifted toward fentanyl and polysubstance use. I combine county-level treatment-center measures with National Vital Statistics System mortality data from 1999 through 2022, replicate estimates from the early epidemic, and apply methods suited to heterogeneous, non-binary treatment. The protective relationship found in earlier years weakens over time, highlighting the difficulty of measuring treatment access as treatment capacity and the drug supply evolve simultaneously.</p>

### The Deterrence Impacts of Fentanyl Supply Laws

**Working paper** · Available upon request

<p class="paper-abstract">This paper studies California Assembly Bill 701, which extended drug-weight sentencing enhancements to fentanyl and increased penalties above one kilogram. State-level synthetic-control estimates provide little evidence that the law reduced aggregate drug activity. Incident-level estimates show a shift away from quantities above the threshold and toward lower-weight incidents, with no meaningful effect on overdose mortality.</p>
:::

![Estimated effects of California Assembly Bill 701](images/research/ab701.png)
